crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: The AI Enablement Audit
children.blurb: The AI Enablement Audit is a structured review of how an organisation adopts, deploys and governs artificial intelligence across its business functions.

children.name: Threat Modelling for Legal AI
children.blurb: Threat modelling for legal AI is the practice of identifying what can go wrong when a law firm or in-house team puts a model into a legal workflow, and who or what could cause it.

children.name: Data Loss Prevention and Sanitisation
children.blurb: Data loss prevention and sanitisation covers the controls that stop sensitive information leaving an organisation and the processes that strip or mask it when data must be shared, reused or tested.

children.name: Shadow AI in Legal Teams
children.blurb: Shadow AI in legal teams covers the use of artificial intelligence tools by lawyers, paralegals and legal operations staff without the knowledge or approval of the firm's IT, security or general counsel function.

sections.body: This section covers the security and enablement work that sits between a legal team and the AI tools it wants to use. In practice that means auditing what a firm already runs, modelling how a legal model could be attacked or leak, keeping confidential material out of the wrong places, finding tools staff adopted on their own, and testing whether outputs treat people fairly. The work is concrete: reviewing configurations, tracing data flows, writing test prompts, and documenting findings for the people who own the risk. It is closer to IT assurance and compliance review than to courtroom advocacy, though the stakes are legal privilege and client confidentiality.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts are mature. Data loss prevention has decades of practice behind it, and sanitisation techniques for text are reasonably well understood, even if generative models make them harder. Threat modelling borrows from established security methods and adapts them to legal workflows, which works but is still being refined. Bias testing is the least settled: there is no single accepted measure of fairness, results depend heavily on the prompts and datasets used, and a clean test does not prove a system is unbiased. Shadow AI is a moving target because staff adoption outpaces policy, and enablement audits often find more than the firm expected. The honest limit across all of it is that audits capture a moment, not a guarantee.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here build on each other in roughly the order a firm would work through them. The AI Enablement Audit is the entry point, setting out how to inventory tools, owners and data flows before anything else makes sense. Threat Modelling for Legal AI takes that inventory and asks how each system could fail or be abused, which is where privilege and confidentiality risks get named. Data Loss Prevention and Sanitisation then deals with the practical controls, covering what leaves a system and how sensitive text is handled. Shadow AI in Legal Teams addresses the tools nobody declared, which is often the gap an audit exposes. Bias Testing and Alignment closes the set by examining output quality and fairness, the part least reducible to a checklist. A reader new to the area should start with the audit page, while someone already running a programme will get most from the threat modelling and bias testing pages.
